scenes.tts: The first film traced inherited information to D N A. How can D N A make a copy? The clue is not the helix shape by itself. It is the matching rule inside a duplex. We will carry the first film's blue D N A into a picture made only of labelled blocks.
scenes.caption: The first film traced inherited information to DNA. How can DNA make a copy? The clue is not the helix shape by itself. It is the matching rule inside a duplex. We will carry the first film's blue DNA into a picture made only of labelled blocks.
scenes.visual: Reuse film one colors: DNA blue and protein gold. Add green outlines only for newly built DNA. Begin with the final blue evidence paths from film one entering from the left and merging into one large blue duplex icon made from two rails and labelled blocks. Put the question above it. Mark the duplex 'schematic' and keep the rails gently turning.

scenes.visual: Transform the question into the title 'How One Strand Specifies Another' for two seconds. Keep the large schematic blue rails turning behind the title, then return them to full contrast.

scenes.tts: Start with base composition, the percentages of adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine. Across double-stranded samples, adenine lies close to thymine, while guanine lies close to cytosine. A model must explain both matches while allowing different samples to carry different base sequences.

scenes.visual: Unroll the blue rails into a full-frame bar ledger. Four labelled blocks, A, T, G and C, pour into bars. Animate A and T to matching heights and G and C to matching heights. Then change all four heights together for a second schematic sample while preserving each pairwise match. Label both examples 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Place two blue rails side by side, running in opposite directions. In canonical Watson-Crick pairing, adenine pairs with thymine, and guanine pairs with cytosine. The paired blocks explain the whole-duplex ratios. The rails are schematic, not molecular structures.

scenes.visual: Transform the bars into two thick blue rails filling most of the frame. Arrowheads on the rails point in opposite directions. A blocks slide into matching T cups; G blocks slide into matching C cups. Reject no base with a certainty mark; instead, only compatible cups close. Keep 'schematic' visible and show no bonds, atoms or molecular geometry.
scenes.narration: Place two blue rails side by side, running in opposite directions. In canonical Watson-Crick pairing, adenine pairs with thymine, and guanine pairs with cytosine. The paired blocks explain the whole-duplex ratios. The rails are schematic, not molecular structures.

scenes.tts: Now unzip one short rail, leaving its partner positions empty. The old blocks remain blue. New blocks will arrive with green outlines. Predict the new partner for the sequence shown on screen. Remember, adenine selects thymine, and guanine selects cytosine. Which blocks fill the empty rail?

Place six empty green-outline cups opposite it, with the opposite-direction arrow already visible. End on the question with the old rail gently drifting and no answer blocks present.

scenes.visual: Hold the blue 5'-GATTAC-3' rail, six empty green-outline positions and the question for 4.5 seconds. Let compatible loose blocks drift around the edge without entering any cup.

scenes.tts: Each position admits its complementary block. The second rail is therefore specified by the first, not guessed. Reverse the reading direction, because the two strands are antiparallel. When both old rails separate, each can guide one new partner. One duplex can therefore become two matching duplexes.

scenes.visual: Green-outline C, T, A, A, T and G blocks enter the empty cups one by one, producing 3'-CTAATG-5' opposite the old rail. Then restore both original blue rails, separate them, and build one green-outline partner beside each. Keep old blue and new green clearly distinct as the two duplexes move apart.

scenes.tts: That is a copying proposal, not yet an experiment. It predicts that every daughter duplex keeps one old strand and receives one new strand. Give old strands a heavy marker and new strands a light marker. Their combined density can reveal which strands stay together.

scenes.visual: Transform the two duplex cartoons into paired strand bars. Add a dark-blue 'heavy' badge to old strands and a pale-green 'light' badge to new strands. Slide each duplex above a vertical density tube with heavy at the bottom and light at the top. Mark both the strand cartoons and the band positions 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Before transfer, D N A forms a heavy band. After one generation in light nitrogen, every duplex should contain one heavy and one light strand. That gives one hybrid band. After another generation, half the duplexes remain hybrid, while half contain two light strands.
scenes.caption: Before transfer, DNA forms a heavy band. After one generation in light nitrogen, every duplex should contain one heavy and one light strand. That gives one hybrid band. After another generation, half the duplexes remain hybrid, while half contain two light strands.
scenes.visual: Use three fixed schematic density tubes labelled before transfer, first generation and second generation. Animate a band at the heavy position, then one at the midpoint hybrid position, then equal-area bands at hybrid and light positions. Above each tube, keep the matching old/new strand bars moving into their band. Show generation numbers only on screen.
scenes.narration: Before transfer, DNA forms a heavy band. After one generation in light nitrogen, every duplex should contain one heavy and one light strand. That gives one hybrid band. After another generation, half the duplexes remain hybrid, while half contain two light strands.

scenes.tts: If parental strands stayed together, separate heavy and light bands would appear after the first generation. If old material dispersed through both strands, one band would shift gradually. The observed hybrid band, followed by hybrid and light bands, matched strand retention. The pattern, not exact density, is the test.

scenes.visual: Keep the observed tubes centered. Brief schematic alternatives slide in at the sides: separate heavy/light bands and one gradually shifting band. Fade those alternatives without stamping 'rejected'. Brighten the observed hybrid, then hybrid-plus-light pattern and connect it to the old-blue/new-green duplex cartoons. Label every band layout 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Pairing does two jobs in this model. It explains why complementary bases match across a duplex, and it lets each old strand specify a new sequence. The density bands test whether each daughter keeps one parental strand. They do not test every enzyme step. Structure supplied a rule; experiment tested its consequence.

A thin line connects the two panels through the same pairing cups. Keep the density pattern as a small schematic inset until the final sentence, then clear it.
